verses.translation: And to the messenger{H4397} of the assembly{H5712} of Ephesus, write{H3789}: Thus{H3541} says{H559} the one who has{H3426} in his right{H3225} hand{H3027} the seven{H7651} stars{H3556}, who walks{H1980} in the midst{H8432} of the seven{H7651} menorot{H4501} of gold{H2091}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses עֵדָה (edah, H5712 — 'assembly/congregation'), the specific term for the congregation of Israel in the wilderness (Num 27:17, Josh 22:16-17, Ex 12:3). Greek uses ἐκκλησία ('church/assembly'). A back-translator from Greek would use קָהָל (qahal — 'assembly') — the standard LXX equivalent. The author uses the Mosaic edah, binding the assemblies of Revelation to the wilderness community.

Uses מְנוֹרוֹת (menorot, H4501) — plural of menorah, the seven-branched lampstand of the Tabernacle (Exodus 25:31-37). Greek has λυχνίας ('lampstands' — generic). A back-translator from Greek would use נֵרוֹת (nerot — 'lamps') or the generic מְאוֹרוֹת (me'orot), not the Temple-specific menorot. The author thinks in Tabernacle categories.

Uses כֹּה אָמַר (koh amar — 'thus says', H3541 + H559) — THE standard prophetic messenger formula used hundreds of times by Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, and Amos (כה אמר יהוה — 'thus says YHWH'). Greek has τάδε λέγει. While this could be a translation, no back-translator would consistently choose the precise OT prophetic formula. Each of the four assembly messages opens with this formula, treating them as prophetic oracles.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'walks in the midst of' (הולך בתוך). Greek: 'walks in the middle of' (περιπατοῦντος ἐν μέσῳ). Close correspondence, but the Hebrew הלך has connotations of God 'walking' in Eden (Gen 3:8 — מִתְהַלֵּךְ בַּגָּן) and in the camp (Deut 23:15).
translation_notes: 'Menorot' (not 'lampstands') to preserve the Temple connection. These are not generic lamps but the menorah of the sanctuary.
'Assembly' for edah rather than 'church' — the Hebrew term carries Mosaic-covenant overtones absent from the Greek ἐκκλησία.
textual_notes: The seven menorot echo Zechariah 4:2 where a single menorah with seven lamps represents YHWH's eyes surveying the earth. Here, seven distinct menorot represent seven assemblies — the imagery is expanded but rooted in Zechariah.

verses.translation: I know{H3045} your deeds{H4639} and your hopes{H8615}, and that you cannot{H3201} bear{H5445} the wicked{H7563}, and you tested{H5254} those who say{H559} they are prophets{H5030} and they are not, and you found{H4672} them to be liars.

one_way_hebrew: Uses תִּקְוָה (tiqvah — 'hope/expectation', H8615) where Greek has both κόπον ('labor') and ὑπομονήν ('patience/endurance'). Tiqvah is the Hebrew concept of hope — the same word Rachel uses naming her son (Gen 30:7), the same word in Jeremiah 29:11 ('a future and a tiqvah'). A back-translator from Greek would use עָמָל (amal — 'labor') and סַבְלָנוּת (savlanut — 'patience'), not the theologically loaded tiqvah. The Hebrew author sees HOPE where the Greek sees ENDURANCE — fundamentally different spiritual perspectives.

Uses נְבִיאִים (nevi'im — 'prophets', H5030) where Greek has ἀποστόλους ('apostles'). This is a major divergence. A back-translator from Greek would use שְׁלוּחִים (sheluchim — 'sent-ones/apostles') as in Rev 21:14. The Hebrew author uses the OT category (prophets) rather than the NT category (apostles). The false claim tested here is prophetic authority, not apostolic commission.

Uses הָרְשָׁעִים (ha-resha'im — 'the wicked', H7563) — the specific Torah-judicial term for the guilty/wicked (Deut 25:1, Ps 1:1, Prov 10:3). Greek has τοὺς κακούς ('evil ones' — morally bad). A back-translator would use הרעים (ha-ra'im — 'the evil'), not the legal-forensic resha'im.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'your hopes' (תקותיך — single word). Greek: 'your labor and your patience' (κόπον καὶ ὑπομονήν — two words). The Hebrew condenses two Greek concepts into one Hebrew concept.
Hebrew: 'prophets' (נביאים). Greek: 'apostles' (ἀποστόλους). Entirely different category of false claim.
Hebrew: כזבנים (kazbanim — 'liars'). This is a characteristically Hebrew agentive form from כזב (kazav — 'to lie'). No standard Strong's number — a later Hebrew formation.
translation_notes: 'Hopes' for tiqvah — not 'patience.' The Hebrew text commends their hope, not their endurance.
'Wicked' for resha'im — a judicial verdict, not merely a moral description. These are the 'guilty' in a Torah court.
textual_notes: Deuteronomy 18:20-22 provides the test for false prophets: if the word does not come to pass, the prophet has spoken presumptuously. The Hebrew's use of 'prophets' (not 'apostles') grounds this in the Deuteronomy standard.

verses.translation: And your hope{H8615} and your labors{H2960}, all{H3605} of it is for the sake of my name{H8034}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses טִרְחָה (tirchah — 'labor/burden', H2960) — from the root used in Deuteronomy 1:12 where Moses says 'How can I alone bear your burden (טרחכם) and your load and your strife?' Greek has no direct equivalent here; this verse's content is redistributed across Greek vv2-3. The Hebrew word carries overtones of Moses's burden-bearing leadership.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'your hope and your labors, all of it is for my name's sake' — concise summary. Greek: 'you have patience, and have borne for my name's sake, and have not grown weary' — expanded with 'not grown weary' (οὐ κεκοπίακες), absent from Hebrew.

verses.translation: But a wonder{H8539} is to me: why{H6440} do you abandon{H5800} the first{H7223} love{H160}?

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses תְּמִיָּה (temiyah — 'wonder/astonishment') — divine amazement. Greek has ἔχω κατὰ σοῦ ('I have against you') — a legal accusation. The Hebrew expresses WONDER: 'I am amazed at you — why?' The Greek expresses JUDGMENT: 'I have a charge against you.' A back-translator from Greek would write יֵשׁ לִי עָלֶיךָ ('I have against you'), not temiyah. The Hebrew reveals divine pathos — God is astonished at the abandonment of love, not merely issuing a legal complaint. This is unique to the Hebrew.

Uses מִפְּנֵי מַה (mipnei mah — 'because of what / why') — a distinctly Hebrew interrogative construction (lit. 'from the face of what'). Greek has ὅτι ('that/because'). A back-translator from Greek would use כִּי (ki — 'because'), not this Hebraic idiom.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'a wonder is to me: why do you abandon?' — expresses divine astonishment. Greek: 'I have against you, that you have left' — expresses divine accusation. Fundamentally different emotional register.
translation_notes: 'Abandon' for ta'azov (H5800) — the root עזב means to forsake/abandon, used of forsaking God (Jer 1:16, 2:13, 17, 19, 5:7) and of God's covenant being forsaken (Deut 29:24, 1 Kings 19:10). This is covenant-forsaking language.
textual_notes: Jeremiah 2:2 — 'I remember the devotion (חֶסֶד) of your youth, the love (אַהֲבָה) of your betrothal, when you followed me in the wilderness.' The 'first love' echoes Jeremiah's imagery of Israel's first love for YHWH.

verses.translation: Remember{H2142} who{H4310} you are and make{H6213} repentance{H7725}, and do{H6213} your first{H7223} deeds{H4639}. And if not, swiftly{H4120} your menorah{H4501} shall be pushed{H1920} from its place{H4725}, if you do not make repentance.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Hebrew says 'remember WHO YOU ARE' (זכור מי אתה). Greek says 'remember FROM WHERE YOU HAVE FALLEN' (μνημόνευε πόθεν πέπτωκας). These are fundamentally different commands: the Hebrew calls for remembering IDENTITY; the Greek calls for remembering the HEIGHT OF THE FALL. A back-translator from Greek would write זכור מאין נפלת ('remember from where you fell'), not מי אתה ('who you are'). The Hebrew focuses on covenantal identity, the Greek on spiritual descent.

Uses תְּשׁוּבָה (teshuvah — 'repentance/return', H8666, from root שוב H7725). This is THE Hebrew concept of repentance — a physical turning back and returning to God. Greek μετανόησον means 'change your mind.' Hebrew teshuvah is bodily return; Greek metanoia is mental transformation. A back-translator would not choose the Hebrew theological term teshuvah to render metanoia.

Uses יִדָּחֵף (yidachef — 'shall be pushed/shoved', H1920) — a violent physical verb used of pushing someone into danger (Ps 118:13, Prov 10:3). Greek κινήσω means simply 'remove/move.' A back-translator from Greek would use אָסִיר (asir — 'I will remove') or אָזִיז (aziz — 'I will move'), not the violent דחף.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'remember who you are' (identity). Greek: 'remember from where you have fallen' (location/status). Entirely different object of memory.
Hebrew: 'your menorah shall be pushed' (passive — by an unnamed agent). Greek: 'I will remove your lampstand' (active — first person). Different agency.
Hebrew uses תשובה twice — opening and closing the warning with the same word, creating an inclusio.
translation_notes: 'Repentance' for teshuvah — literally 'return.' The Hebrew concept of repentance is a journey home, not merely a change of opinion.
'Pushed' for yidachef — the menorah will be forcibly displaced, not gently moved.
textual_notes: The phrase 'remember who you are' recalls Deuteronomy 5:15 and 8:2 — Israel commanded to 'remember' their identity as redeemed slaves. This is covenantal memory.

verses.translation: Whoever{H4310} has{H3426} ears{H241} hears{H8085} what the Spirit{H7307} says{H559} to the assembly{H5712}. Whoever overcomes{H5329} shall eat{H398} from the tree{H6086} of life{H2416} which is in the Garden{H1588} of Eden{H5731}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses גַּן עֵדֶן (Gan Eden — 'Garden of Eden', H1588 + H5731) — the specific Genesis 2:8-15 designation. Greek has ἐν τῷ παραδείσῳ τοῦ θεοῦ ('in the Paradise of God'). The word 'paradise' (παράδεισος) is itself a Persian loanword that entered Greek. A back-translator from Greek would use פַּרְדֵּס (pardes — 'paradise/garden') — the Hebrew source of the Greek word — NOT the Genesis-specific Gan Eden. The Hebrew author thinks in Torah geography: the overcomer returns to the Garden of Eden. The Greek translator converted this to the generic 'Paradise.' This is among the strongest one-way markers in the chapter.

Uses אָזְנַיִם (oznayim — 'ears', DUAL form) where Greek has singular οὖς ('ear'). The Hebrew naturally uses the dual for paired body parts. More significantly, the Hebrew שׁוֹמֵעַ (shome'a) is a PARTICIPLE ('hears' — a statement of fact) while the Greek ἀκουσάτω is an IMPERATIVE ('let him hear' — a command). In the Hebrew, having ears means you necessarily hear; in the Greek, having an ear requires a choice to listen.

Uses עֵץ הַחַיִּים (ets ha-chayyim — 'tree of life', H6086 + H2416) — the exact phrase from Genesis 2:9, 3:22,24. Greek τοῦ ξύλου τῆς ζωῆς corresponds, but the Hebrew carries the entire Genesis narrative of the forbidden tree now restored to the overcomer.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'Garden of Eden' (geographic Genesis location). Greek: 'Paradise of God' (theological abstraction). Different designation entirely.

Hebrew lacks the content of standard Greek v6 ('But this you have, that you hate the works of the Nicolaitans, which I also hate'). This Nicolaitan reference in the Ephesus message is entirely absent from the Hebrew. The Hebrew places the Nicolaitan commendation in the Pergamos section instead (v14).
translation_notes: 'Garden of Eden' — not 'Paradise' — preserving the Genesis geography. The overcomer's reward is access to the original garden.
The Hebrew 'hears' (participle/indicative) rather than 'let him hear' (imperative) transforms the formula from a command into a declaration.
textual_notes: Genesis 3:22-24 — Adam was expelled from the garden and the way to the tree of life was guarded by cherubim. The overcomer's promise reverses the Genesis exile — access to the tree of life is restored.

verses.translation: And to the messenger{H4397} of the assembly{H5712} of Zmirinin, write{H3789}: Thus{H3541} says{H559} the first{H7223} and the last{H314}, the dead{H4191} one who rose{H6965}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses הָרִאשׁוֹן וְהָאַחֲרוֹן (ha-rishon ve-ha-acharon — 'the first and the last') — a direct quotation from Isaiah 44:6 and 48:12 where YHWH declares 'I am the first and I am the last.' The same Isaiah formula appeared in Rev 21:6. Greek has ὁ πρῶτος καὶ ὁ ἔσχατος, which corresponds but lacks the Isaiah resonance.

Uses וְקָם (ve-qam — 'and arose/rose', H6965) — the standard Hebrew resurrection verb, terse and powerful: two syllables. Greek has ἔζησεν ('came to life'). The Hebrew קום is used throughout the OT for rising/standing (rising from death in Isa 26:19 — יְקוּמוּן 'they shall rise'). A back-translator from Greek would more likely use וְחַי (ve-chai — 'and lived').

The construction הַמֵּת וְקָם ('the dead-one and rose') is characteristically Hebraic in its terse juxtaposition of death and resurrection in three words. Greek expands this: ὃς ἐγένετο νεκρός καὶ ἔζησεν ('who became dead and came to life') — six words.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'Zmirinin' (זמירנין) — an Aramaic-influenced transliteration with the -in suffix. Greek: 'Smyrna' (Σμύρναν). The Hebrew form suggests the name was heard and rendered through a Semitic ear.
translation_notes: 'The dead one who rose' — preserving the Hebrew terse construction. The participle ha-met ('the dead one') and the perfect ve-qam ('and rose') compress the entire death-and-resurrection event into minimal words.
textual_notes: Isaiah 44:6 — 'Thus says YHWH, the King of Israel, and his Redeemer, YHWH of Hosts: I am the first, and I am the last; besides me there is no God.' The speaker identifies with YHWH's self-declaration.

verses.translation: I know{H3045} your deeds{H4639} and your distresses, and the reproach{H2778} from those who say{H559} that they are Yehudim{H3064} and they are not, but they are of the children{H1121} of the Adversary{H7854}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses מִבְּנֵי הַשָּׂטָן (mi-bnei ha-Satan — 'of the children of the Adversary'). Greek has συναγωγὴ τοῦ Σατανᾶ ('synagogue of Satan'). These are entirely different metaphors: the Hebrew uses a FAMILIAL image (children of), the Greek an INSTITUTIONAL image (synagogue of). A back-translator from Greek would write בֵּית כְּנֶסֶת הַשָּׂטָן ('synagogue of the Satan'), not 'children of the Satan.' The Hebrew metaphor echoes 'children of Belial' (בני בליעל — Deut 13:14, Judg 19:22, 1 Sam 2:12) — a Hebrew idiom for the wicked.

Uses הַשָּׂטָן (ha-Satan — 'the Adversary/Accuser', H7854) with the definite article — exactly as in Job 1:6-7, 2:1-2 where 'the Satan' is a TITLE/ROLE, not a proper name. Greek Σατανᾶ is used as a proper name without article. The Hebrew preserves the OT functional title.

Uses חֵירוּף (cheiruf — 'reproach/scorn', from root H2778) where Greek has βλασφημίαν ('blasphemy'). A back-translator from Greek would use גִּדּוּף (gidduf — 'blasphemy/cursing'). The Hebrew cheiruf specifically means 'taunting/reproach' — as in Goliath's reproach of Israel (1 Sam 17:26 — חֵרֵף מַעַרְכוֹת אלהים חיים 'he reproached the ranks of the living God').
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'children of the Adversary' (familial metaphor). Greek: 'synagogue of Satan' (institutional metaphor). Different imagery entirely.
Hebrew: 'reproach' (חירוף). Greek: 'blasphemy' (βλασφημία). Different offense — reproach is horizontal (against people), blasphemy is vertical (against God).
Hebrew omits: 'and poverty (but you are rich)' (καὶ τὴν πτωχείαν, πλούσιος δὲ εἶ) — the entire poverty/riches paradox from Greek is absent.
translation_notes: 'Adversary' for ha-Satan preserves the Hebrew title-meaning. Ha-Satan is 'the Accuser' — a courtroom role.
'Yehudim' rather than 'Jews' — preserving the Hebrew self-designation linked to Yehudah (Judah).
textual_notes: The phrase 'children of' (בני) as a character description is a classic Hebraism: 'children of Belial' (worthless sons), 'children of light,' 'children of darkness.' This construction has no natural Greek equivalent.

verses.translation: Do not fear{H3372} them. See{H7200}! The Adversary{H7854} shall take{H3947} some of you in captivity{H7633}, in order to test{H5254} you, and the distress shall be to you ten{H6235} days{H3117}. Be faithful{H539} until{H5704} the day{H3117} of your death{H4194}, so that I give{H5414} you the crown{H3804} of life{H2416}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses שִׁבְיָה (shivyah — 'captivity', H7633) where Greek has φυλακήν ('prison'). Shivyah is the Hebrew concept of being taken captive — the word for exile and captivity (Deut 21:10, 2 Chron 28:11, Neh 1:2-3). This carries the weight of the Babylonian captivity. A back-translator from Greek would use בֵּית הָאֲסוּרִים (beit ha-asurim — 'prison/house of binding') or כֶּלֶא (kele — 'prison'), not the exile-captivity term shivyah.

Uses כֶּתֶר (keter — 'crown', H3804) — the specific word for a royal diadem/crown, used only in Esther (1:11, 2:17, 6:8). Greek has στέφανον (stephanos — 'wreath/garland crown'). A stephanos is a victory wreath given to athletes and military victors; a keter is a royal crown worn by monarchs. A back-translator from Greek would use עֲטָרָה (atarah — 'wreath/crown') which better corresponds to stephanos. The Hebrew author grants a ROYAL crown, not a victory wreath.

Uses יִקַּח (yiqqach — 'shall take/seize', H3947) where Greek has μέλλει βάλλειν ('is about to cast/throw'). Different actions: the Hebrew implies seizing/capturing; the Greek implies violently throwing into prison.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'captivity' (שביה — exile imagery). Greek: 'prison' (φυλακή — incarceration imagery). Different concepts of confinement.
Hebrew: 'crown' (כתר — royal diadem). Greek: 'crown' (στέφανος — victory wreath). Different types of crown.

Hebrew: 'the Adversary shall take some of you in captivity.' Greek: 'the devil is about to throw some of you into prison.' Different agent name (Adversary vs. devil), different action (take vs. throw).
Note: [מכם] ('of you') appears in brackets in the source text, indicating editorial restoration.
translation_notes: 'Crown' for keter — a royal crown, not a competition wreath. The overcomer receives kingship.
'Captivity' for shivyah — not mere imprisonment but exile-captivity, with all its theological resonance.
textual_notes: Daniel 1:12-15 — Daniel's ten-day test period is the closest OT parallel to 'ten days' of testing. The Hebrew reader would naturally connect this to Daniel's faithfulness under foreign captivity.

verses.translation: Whoever{H4310} has{H3426} ears{H241} hears{H8085} what the Spirit{H7307} says{H559} to the assembly{H5712}. Whoever overcomes{H5329} shall not have distress from another{H312} death{H4194}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses מָוֶת אַחֶרֶת (mavet acheret — 'another/different death') rather than merely 'second death.' The Hebrew אַחֶרֶת (acheret, H312) means 'another/different/other' (feminine of אַחֵר) — implying a death of a DIFFERENT KIND, not simply 'the second in sequence.' Greek has θανάτου τοῦ δευτέρου ('the second death'), using an ordinal number. A back-translator from Greek would write מיתה שניה (mitah sheniyah — 'second death'), not acheret. The Hebrew implies qualitative difference; the Greek implies sequential numbering.
Uses צַעַר (tsa'ar — 'distress/pain') where Greek has ἀδικηθῇ ('be harmed/injured'). Different concept: Hebrew speaks of suffering; Greek speaks of being wronged/harmed.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'shall not have distress from another death.' Greek: 'shall not be hurt by the second death.' Different preposition, different qualifier (another vs. second), different verb (have distress vs. be harmed).
translation_notes: 'Another death' (not 'second death') to preserve the Hebrew acheret's meaning of qualitative difference.

verses.translation: And to the messenger{H4397} of the assembly{H5712} of Pergamos, write{H3789}: Thus{H3541} says{H559} the one who has{H3426} a sword{H2719} of edges{H6366}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses חֶרֶב פִּיפִיּוֹת (cherev pifiyot — 'sword of edges/mouths', H2719 + H6366) — a DIRECT QUOTE from Psalm 149:6 (וְחֶרֶב פִּיפִיּוֹת בְּיָדָם — 'and a two-edged sword in their hand'). Greek has ῥομφαίαν τὴν δίστομον τὴν ὀξεῖαν ('the sharp two-mouthed sword'). A back-translator from Greek might write חרב חדה ('sharp sword'). The Hebrew author reaches for the Psalm's exact phrase. Note: פיפיות is from פֶּה (peh — 'mouth'), so literally 'sword of mouths' — double-mouthed/double-edged.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'sword of edges' (cherev pifiyot — Psalm quotation). Greek adds 'sharp' (ὀξεῖαν) which is absent from the Hebrew.
Hebrew: 'Pergamos' rendered as פירגימום (Pergeimom) — a Semitic transliteration.
translation_notes: 'Sword of edges' preserves the Psalm 149:6 connection. The word pifiyot ('edges/mouths') implies the sword cuts in both directions.
textual_notes: Psalm 149:6 — 'Let the high praises of God be in their mouth, and a two-edged sword (cherev pifiyot) in their hand.' The connection between praise and the sword is preserved: the sword comes from the mouth (v15).

verses.translation: I know{H3045} your deeds{H4639}, and your place{H4725} is in a place{H4725} where there is the throne{H3678} of the Adversary{H7854}, and you believe{H539} in my name{H8034} and in my faithfulness{H530}. And in the time{H6256} my faithful{H539} companion{H2270} Antipas was killed{H2026} among you, in the place where the Adversary dwells{H1752}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses חֲבֵרִי (chaveri — 'my companion/friend', H2270) for Antipas. Greek has μάρτυς μου ὁ πιστός ('my faithful witness/martyr'). A back-translator from Greek would use עֵדִי (edi — 'my witness'). The Hebrew reveals a personal relationship: Antipas is not merely a witness giving testimony but a companion — an intimate friend. The word חָבֵר appears in Judges 20:11, Psalm 45:8, Song 1:7, and Proverbs 28:24.

Uses אֱמוּנָה (emunah — 'faithfulness', H530) — from the same root as אָמֵן (amen). The Hebrew word encompasses both 'faith' AND 'faithfulness' — they are inseparable in Hebrew thought. Greek splits this into πίστις ('faith') and πιστός ('faithful'). The Hebrew 'in my faithfulness' (be-emunati) means 'in the faithfulness that I have and that you share in' — both objective and subjective senses at once.

Uses כִּסֵּא (kiseh — 'throne', H3678) — the same word for YHWH's throne (Ps 11:4, Isa 6:1). The Adversary has a counterfeit throne. Greek uses θρόνος, which corresponds, but the Hebrew kiseh carries the weight of Israel's throne tradition.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'my companion' (חבירי — personal relationship). Greek: 'my witness/martyr' (μάρτυς — testimony role). Different description of Antipas.

Hebrew: 'you believe in my name and in my faithfulness' (positive affirmation). Greek: 'you hold fast my name and did not deny my faith' (double negative/positive). Different framing — Hebrew affirms belief, Greek denies denial.
Hebrew: 'in the time... was killed' — passive construction without specifying the killers. Greek: similar passive but the Hebrew is more terse.
translation_notes: 'Companion' for chaveri — not 'witness' or 'martyr.' The Hebrew reveals intimacy.
'Faithfulness' for emunah — this single word carries both the faith OF the believer and the faithfulness OF Messiah.
textual_notes: The phrase 'throne of the Adversary' echoes the counterfeit-throne imagery found in Isaiah 14:13 where the aspirant says 'I will set my throne above the stars of God.'

verses.translation: And also you hate{H8130} those who learn{H3925} the teaching{H3948} of Bilam{H1109}, who taught{H3925} by the hand{H3027} of Balaq{H1111} to do{H6213} evil{H7451} to the children{H1121} of Yisrael{H3478}, to cause them to sin{H2398} in fornication{H2184}.

one_way_hebrew: MAJOR STRUCTURAL DEVIATION: The Hebrew PRAISES Pergamos for HATING the Balaam teaching ('and also you hate those who learn the teaching of Bilam'). The Greek CHARGES Pergamos with TOLERATING it ('I have against you... you have there those who hold the teaching of Balaam'). This is a diametrically opposite assessment. A back-translator from Greek, which criticizes the church, would never produce a commendation.

Uses עַל יַד (al yad — 'by the hand of', H5921 + H3027) — a Hebrew idiom for agency/instrumentality (1 Kings 16:12, Jer 37:2). Greek has ὃς ἐδίδαξεν τί Βαλάκ ('who taught Balak'). The Hebrew construction says Bilam taught THROUGH/BY MEANS OF Balaq — Balaq was the instrument, Bilam the instigator. The Greek says Bilam taught Balak directly.

Uses לַחֲטוֹא (lachato — 'to cause to sin', causative of H2398) — the specific hifil form meaning to lead into sin, used of Jeroboam who 'caused Israel to sin' (1 Kings 14:16, 15:26, 16:2). Greek has πορνεῦσαι ('to commit fornication'). The Hebrew verb is broader — causing sin — while the Greek specifies the type.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'you hate those who learn' (commendation). Greek: 'you have there those who hold' (accusation). Opposite assessment.

Hebrew: 'to do evil to the children of Israel, to cause them to sin in fornication.' Greek: 'to cast a stumbling block before the children of Israel, to eat things sacrificed to idols and to commit fornication.' Hebrew omits 'eating idol-sacrifices' and 'stumbling block.'
Hebrew: uses בלעם (Bil'am) — the Hebrew form. Greek: Βαλαάμ (Balaam) — the Hellenized form.
translation_notes: 'Bilam' — using the Hebrew pronunciation rather than the Hellenized 'Balaam.'
'To cause them to sin' — the causative hifil form places the blame on the teacher, not the sinners.
textual_notes: Numbers 25:1-3 and 31:16 — Bilam's counsel led to Israel's fornication with Moabite women at Shittim. The Hebrew author draws directly on the Torah narrative.

verses.translation: And also you hate{H8130} the teaching{H3948} of the Nicolaitans; and even{H637} I hate{H8130} those.

one_way_hebrew: The phrase וְאַף אֲנִי שׂוֹנֵא מֵאֵילּוּ ('and even I hate those') — God's personal hatred of the Nicolaitans — is absent from the standard Greek text of the Pergamos letter. In the Greek, the Nicolaitan hatred appears only in the Ephesus letter (Rev 2:6 — ὃ κἀγὼ μισῶ — 'which I also hate'). The Hebrew relocates this divine hatred to Pergamos and combines it with the Balaam commendation, creating a unified passage of praise for rejecting false teaching.

The Hebrew text places the Nicolaitan reference in the Pergamos section, while the Greek text places it in the Ephesus section (Greek v6). A back-translator following the Greek order would never relocate this material. The different structural placement suggests an independent textual tradition.
greek_deviations: In the Greek, the Pergamos letter CRITICIZES the church for having Nicolaitans (Rev 2:15 — 'So you also have those who hold the teaching of the Nicolaitans'). The Hebrew PRAISES the church for hating them. Opposite evaluation.
The phrase 'and even I hate those' corresponds to Greek Rev 2:6 (Ephesus letter), not to the Pergamos letter. The Hebrew has moved this material between letters.
translation_notes: The Nicolaitan reference uses a Hebraicized transliteration: ניקאלטציאן — suggesting the name was heard and rendered through Hebrew phonology.

verses.translation: Make{H6213} repentance{H7725}! And if not, I will come{H935} swiftly{H4120} to make{H6213} war{H4421} with you by means of the sword{H2719} that is in my mouth{H6310}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses מִלְחָמָה (milchamah — 'war', H4421) — the standard Hebrew word for warfare/battle (Ex 1:10, 13:17, 14:14). Greek has πολεμήσω ('I will fight/wage war'). While these correspond, the Hebrew noun milchamah carries the weight of YHWH's wars (מלחמות יהוה — 'the wars of YHWH', Num 21:14, 1 Sam 18:17, 25:28).

Uses עַל יַד ('by means of') again — the same Hebrew idiom for instrumentality as in v13. This creates a literary link: Bilam worked evil 'by the hand of' Balaq, and now Messiah wages war 'by the hand of' his sword.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'I will come swiftly to make war with you' — the war is directed at 'you' (the assembly). Greek: 'I will come quickly and fight against THEM with the sword of my mouth' — directed at the offenders (αὐτῶν — 'them'), not the whole church. Different target of judgment.
Hebrew: 'the sword that is in my mouth' (שיש בפי). Greek: 'the sword of my mouth' (τῆς στόματός μου). Similar but the Hebrew emphasizes the sword's location (it dwells IN the mouth).
translation_notes: Teshuvah again — the Hebrew concept of return/repentance frames the entire Pergamos warning.
textual_notes: Isaiah 49:2 — 'He made my mouth like a sharp sword.' The sword-from-the-mouth image has deep prophetic roots.

verses.translation: Whoever{H4310} has{H3426} ears{H241} hears{H8085} what the Spirit{H7307} says{H559} to the assembly{H5712}. Whoever overcomes{H5329} — I desire{H7521} to give{H5414} him to eat{H398} from the hidden{H5641} manna{H4478}, and also a good{H2896} testimony{H5715}; and in this testimony a new{H2319} name{H8034} is written{H3789}, which none{H3808} can{H3201} read{H7121} except{H7535} the one who received{H6901} it.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses עֵדוּת טוֹבָה (edut tovah — 'good testimony', H5715 + H2896) where Greek has ψῆφον λευκήν ('white stone/pebble'). This is one of the most dramatic one-way markers in the chapter. The Hebrew עֵדוּת is THE word for the Tablets of the Covenant kept inside the Ark (Ex 25:16,21, 31:18, 40:20 — לוּחוֹת הָעֵדוּת 'tablets of the testimony'). The Greek ψῆφος (psephos) is a culturally Greek object — a voting pebble used in courts for acquittal (white) or condemnation (black). A back-translator from Greek would write אֶבֶן לְבָנָה ('white stone'), NOT the covenantal term edut. The Hebrew author gives the overcomer a COVENANTAL TESTIMONY; the Greek translator converted this into a culturally Greek symbol.

REMARKABLE: The Ark of the Covenant contained THREE items: (1) the tablets of testimony (edut), (2) a jar of manna (man), and (3) Aaron's rod (Ex 16:33-34, 25:16, Num 17:25, Heb 9:4). In this single verse, the overcomer receives TWO of the three Ark items: the hidden MANNA and a TESTIMONY. This Ark-of-the-Covenant connection is invisible in the Greek, which has 'hidden manna and a white stone.' No back-translator would accidentally reconstruct the Ark vocabulary.

Uses טוֹבָה (tovah — 'good', H2896) where Greek has λευκήν ('white'). A back-translator from Greek would write לְבָנָה (levanah — 'white'), not tovah. The Hebrew uses a moral/qualitative descriptor ('good'); the Greek uses a color descriptor ('white').

Uses רוֹצֶה אֲנִי (rotzeh ani — 'I desire/want') — expressing divine will/desire. Greek has δώσω ('I will give') — a simple future. The Hebrew reveals divine yearning to bless the overcomer; the Greek merely states the gift.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'a good testimony' (עדות טובה — covenantal object). Greek: 'a white stone' (ψῆφον λευκήν — Greek cultural object). Entirely different metaphor.
Hebrew: 'good' (טובה — moral quality). Greek: 'white' (λευκήν — color). Different descriptor.
Hebrew: 'in this testimony a new name is written.' Greek: 'in the stone a new name written.' The Hebrew has the name written on a testimony; the Greek has it on a stone.
translation_notes: 'Testimony' for edut — preserving the Ark-of-the-Covenant connection. The overcomer receives a covenant document.

'Hidden manna' — the manna hidden in the Ark (Ex 16:33-34), a pot of manna kept 'before the testimony' (לִפְנֵי הָעֵדוּת). The manna and testimony are placed together in the Ark — the Hebrew verse reunites them.
textual_notes: Exodus 16:33-34 — 'Take a jar and put an omer of manna in it, and place it before YHWH, to be kept throughout your generations... Aaron placed it before the Testimony, to be kept.' The hidden manna is literally the manna hidden inside the Ark alongside the testimony — exactly the two items given to the overcomer in this verse.

verses.translation: And to the messenger{H4397} of the assembly{H5712} of Thyatira, write{H3789}: Thus{H3541} says{H559} the Son{H1121} of YHWH{H3068}, whose eyes{H5869} are like a flame{H3851} of fire{H784}, and his feet{H7272} like bronze{H5178}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses בֶּן יַהְוֶה (Ben YHWH — 'Son of YHWH', H1121 + H3068). Greek has ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ θεοῦ ('the Son of God'). This is perhaps the single most theologically significant one-way marker in the entire chapter. A back-translator from Greek would write בֶּן אֱלֹהִים (Ben Elohim — 'Son of God'). The Hebrew preserves the sacred covenantal name YHWH — the name revealed to Moses at the burning bush (Ex 3:14-15). The speaker is not merely 'Son of God' (a title applicable to angels and kings in the OT) but specifically Son of YHWH — Son of the covenant God of Israel.

Uses לַהֶבֶת אֵשׁ (lahevet esh — 'flame of fire', H3851 + H784). This phrase echoes Exodus 3:2 (the burning bush — בְּלַבַּת אֵשׁ) and Song of Songs 8:6 (שַׁלְהֶבֶתְיָה — 'flame of YAH'). Greek has φλόγα πυρός ('flame of fire'). The correspondence is close, but the Hebrew carries the burning-bush and Song of Songs resonance.

Uses נְחוֹשֶׁת (nechoshet — 'bronze/copper', H5178) — the material of the Tabernacle's altar and laver (Ex 27:2, 30:18). Greek has χαλκολιβάνῳ ('fine brass/burnished bronze'). The Hebrew uses the standard OT Tabernacle metal.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'Son of YHWH' (בן יהוה — the divine name). Greek: 'Son of God' (υἱὸς τοῦ θεοῦ — generic title). The Hebrew preserves the sacred name.
Hebrew: כמה כמו ('how much like' — intensified comparison). Greek has no intensifier. The כמה may be an exclamatory particle emphasizing the eyes' fire-like quality.
Greek adds 'fine/burnished' (χαλκολίβανος — a specific alloy). Hebrew simply says 'bronze' (נחושת).
translation_notes: 'Son of YHWH' — not 'Son of God.' The Hebrew preserves the specific divine name that identifies the covenant God of Israel.
The כמה before כמו appears to be an intensifier — 'how exceedingly like a flame of fire' — adding emphasis to the comparison.
textual_notes: Daniel 10:6 — 'his eyes like torches of fire, and his arms and his feet like the gleam of burnished bronze.' The Thyatira description draws directly from Daniel's theophany.

verses.translation: I know{H3045} your deeds{H4639} and your loves{H160} and your service and your faithfulness{H530} and your hopes{H8615}, and in every{H3605} time{H6256} you do{H6213} more{H3148}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses תִּקְוָה (tiqvah — 'hope', H8615) again where Greek has ὑπομονήν ('patience/endurance'). This is a consistent pattern throughout the Hebrew Revelation: where the Greek sees ENDURANCE, the Hebrew sees HOPE. This is a fundamental theological difference that no back-translator would produce.

Uses שֵׁארוּת (she'arut — 'service/ministry') — a Hebrew word for serving that may be related to the root שׁרת (sharet — 'to minister', H8334), the Levitical service word used for priestly ministry (Ex 28:35, Num 1:50, 3:6). Greek has διακονίαν ('service/ministry'). The Hebrew carries priestly overtones.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'in every time you do more' (progressive growth). Greek: 'the last works are more than the first' (τὰ ἔσχατα πλείονα τῶν πρώτων — comparison of first and last). Different framing — the Hebrew sees constant increase, the Greek a before-and-after contrast.
Hebrew: 'your loves' (plural — אהבתיך). Greek: 'your love' (singular — ἀγάπην). The Hebrew acknowledges multiple expressions of love.
translation_notes: 'Hopes' for tiqvah — consistent with v2 and v3. The Hebrew commends hope as a virtue alongside love, service, and faithfulness.
שֵׁארוּת lacks a standard Strong's number. It may be a later Hebrew form from the priestly service root.

verses.translation: But a small{H6996} matter{H1697} I have{H3426} against you: that you tolerate{H5800} the woman{H802} Izevel{H348}, who says{H559} she is a prophetess{H5031}, and they teach{H3925} and entice{H5496} my servants{H5650} to do{H6213} fornication{H2184}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses מַסִּיתִים (masitim — 'enticers', from root סות/סית H5496) — the specific Torah word for enticement to idolatry from Deuteronomy 13:7 (כִּי יְסִיתְךָ אָחִיךָ — 'if your brother entices you'). Greek has πλανᾷ ('deceives/leads astray'). A back-translator from Greek would use מַתְעֶה (mat'eh — 'one who leads astray'), not the Deuteronomy 13 enticement term. The Hebrew author sees Izevel's seduction through the lens of Torah's most severe category of offense — incitement to apostasy.

Uses יִזֶאבֶל (Izevel, H348) — the Hebrew form of the name, directly connecting to the wicked queen of 1 Kings 16:31. The name in Hebrew is thought to contain אִי זְבוּל ('Where is the prince?') — a liturgical cry to Baal. The Hebrew preserves this etymology; the Greek Ἰεζαβήλ is a phonetic rendering that loses the meaning.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'a small matter' (דבר קטון). Greek: 'a few things' (ὀλίγα). Different quantification — Hebrew is singular and diminutive, Greek is plural.

Hebrew: 'that you tolerate' (שתעזוב — from עזב 'to leave/permit'). Greek: 'you suffer/permit' (ἐᾷς). The Hebrew root עזב normally means 'to abandon/forsake,' here used in the sense of 'leaving her alone / not stopping her.'

Hebrew: 'and they teach and entice my servants to do fornication.' Greek: 'to teach and seduce my servants to commit fornication and to eat things sacrificed to idols.' Hebrew omits 'eating idol-sacrifices' — consistently absent throughout this chapter.
translation_notes: 'Entice' for masitim — the Deuteronomy 13 enticement term, the most severe category of religious offense in Torah law.
'Izevel' — the Hebrew pronunciation, preserving the possible Ba'al-liturgy etymology.
textual_notes: 1 Kings 21:25 — 'There was none who sold himself to do evil in the sight of YHWH like Ahab, whom Izevel his wife enticed (הסתה).' The same root סות/סית is used of the original Izevel — the Hebrew Revelation deliberately uses the same verb.

verses.translation: See{H7200}! I am bringing{H935} upon her and upon the one who lies{H7901} with her much distress, if they do not make{H6213} repentance{H7725} concerning their deeds{H4639}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses שֹׁכֵב עִמָּהּ (shochev immah — 'who lies with her', H7901) — the specific Hebrew euphemism for sexual intercourse used throughout Torah law (Gen 19:32, 30:15, 34:2, 39:7, Lev 15:18, 20:11-13, Deut 22:22-25). Greek has τοὺς μοιχεύοντας μετ' αὐτῆς ('those who commit adultery with her'). A back-translator from Greek would use מְנַאֲפִים (mena'afim — 'adulterers'). The Hebrew uses the broader Torah-legal idiom 'lying with,' which covers various sexual offenses, not only adultery.

Uses singular זֶה שֶׁשֹׁכֵב ('this one who lies') — SINGULAR. Greek has plural τοὺς μοιχεύοντας ('those who commit adultery') — PLURAL. The Hebrew singles out one individual; the Greek addresses a group.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'I am bringing upon her much distress.' Greek: 'I will cast her into a bed/sickbed' (βάλλω αὐτὴν εἰς κλίνην). The Greek's 'bed' (κλίνη) metaphor — ironic punishment by sickbed — is entirely absent from the Hebrew.
Hebrew: 'the one who lies with her' (singular). Greek: 'those who commit adultery with her' (plural).
Hebrew: 'if they do not make repentance' (conditional — repentance is still possible). Greek: 'unless they repent of her deeds' (similar conditional).
translation_notes: 'Lies with her' — the Torah-legal euphemism, preserving the connection to Levitical sexual-law categories.

verses.translation: And I gave{H5414} her a time{H6256} to make{H6213} repentance{H7725}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses עֵת (et — 'time/season/appointed time', H6256) — a word carrying the connotation of a divinely appointed moment (Eccl 3:1 — 'a time for every purpose under heaven'). Greek has χρόνον ('time' — duration/chronological time). The Hebrew implies a KAIROS moment — an appointed season for return; the Greek implies a CHRONOS span — a period of time. A back-translator from Greek would use זְמַן (zeman — 'time-span'), not the appointed-moment word et.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: concise — 'I gave her a time to make repentance.' Greek adds: 'of her fornication; and she repented not' (ἐκ τῆς πορνείας αὐτῆς, καὶ οὐ μετενόησεν). The Hebrew omits both the specification 'of her fornication' and the statement 'she repented not.'

verses.translation: And her children{H1121} shall be put to death{H4191}, and all{H3605} the assembly{H5712} shall recognize{H5234} that I am the one who tests{H974} kidneys{H3629} and heart{H3820}; and every{H3605} one{H259} according to his measures{H4060} shall be repaid{H7999}.

one_way_hebrew: DIRECT QUOTATION: הַבּוֹחֵן כְּלָיוֹת וָלֵב (ha-bochen kelayot va-lev — 'the tester of kidneys and heart') is a VERBATIM quote from Jeremiah 11:20 (בֹּחֵן כְּלָיוֹת וָלֵב) and 17:10 (אֲנִי יְהוָה חֹקֵר לֵב בֹּחֵן כְּלָיוֹת — 'I YHWH search the heart, test the kidneys'). See also Psalm 7:10 and Jeremiah 20:12. Greek has ὁ ἐραυνῶν νεφροὺς καὶ καρδίας ('the searcher of kidneys and hearts'). While the Greek corresponds, the Hebrew preserves Jeremiah's exact formula. A back-translator could produce this, but the precise Jeremiah phrasing is more natural as a source than as a translation.

Uses מִדּוֹתָיו (middotav — 'his measures/attributes', H4060) where Greek has ἔργα ('works'). The Hebrew middot is a deeply Jewish concept — character traits, moral qualities, measured attributes. In rabbinic thought, the middot of God (attributes of mercy, justice, etc.) are foundational theology. A back-translator from Greek would use מַעֲשִׂים (ma'asim — 'works/deeds'), not the theologically loaded middot. The Hebrew says each person is repaid according to their CHARACTER, not merely their ACTIONS.

Uses יוּמְתוּ (yumtu — 'shall be put to death', hophal of H4191) — the JUDICIAL DEATH FORMULA from Torah law: מוֹת יוּמָת ('he shall surely be put to death', Gen 2:17, Ex 21:12, Lev 20:2). Greek says ἀποκτενῶ ἐν θανάτῳ ('I will kill with death'). The Hebrew passive (hophal) implies judicial execution by due process; the Greek active first person implies direct killing.

Uses תַּכִּירוּ (takiru — 'shall recognize/discern', H5234 — root נכר) — meaning to identify, acknowledge, recognize by examination. Greek has γνώσονται ('shall know'). The Hebrew implies experiential recognition — they will come to recognize through evidence — while the Greek implies simple knowledge.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'all the assembly' (singular — כל העדה). Greek: 'all the churches' (plural — πᾶσαι αἱ ἐκκλησίαι). The Hebrew maintains its consistent use of edah.
Hebrew: 'according to his measures' (מדותיו — character attributes). Greek: 'according to your works' (τὰ ἔργα ὑμῶν — deeds). Different basis of judgment — character vs. actions.
Hebrew: 'shall be repaid to him' (passive — ישולם לו). Greek: 'I will give to every one of you' (active — δώσω ἑκάστῳ ὑμῶν). Different agency.
translation_notes: 'Put to death' for yumtu — the Torah judicial formula, not merely 'killed.'
'Measures' for middot — character attributes, not mere actions. This is the Hebrew concept of being judged by who you ARE, not only what you DO.

'Kidneys and heart' — in Hebrew anthropology, the kidneys (kelayot) are the seat of deep emotion and conscience, the heart (lev) is the seat of will and thought. Together they represent the total inner person.
textual_notes: Jeremiah 17:10 — 'I YHWH search the heart, test the kidneys, to give to every man according to his ways, according to the fruit of his deeds.' The Jeremiah source includes both testing (בחן) and repaying — the same two elements combined in this verse.

verses.translation: But to you and to the others{H312} who are in Thyatira, I say{H559} that I will not bring{H935} upon you more{H5750} distress, since you do not learn{H3925} from the teaching{H3948} of the Adversary{H7854}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses לִימּוּד הַשָּׂטָן (limmud ha-Satan — 'the teaching of the Adversary', H3948 + H7854) where Greek has τὰ βαθέα τοῦ Σατανᾶ ('the depths of Satan'). These are entirely different concepts: 'teaching' (surface instruction, curriculum) vs. 'depths' (βαθέα — deep things, mysteries). A back-translator from Greek would write עֲמוּקוֹת הַשָּׂטָן ('the deep things of Satan'), not limmud (teaching). The Hebrew sees the Satan as a teacher with a curriculum; the Greek sees hidden esoteric depths.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'the teaching of the Adversary' (לימוד השטן). Greek: 'the depths of Satan' (τὰ βαθέα τοῦ Σατανᾶ). Different metaphor — teaching vs. depths.

Hebrew: 'I will not bring upon you more distress' (שלא אביא עליכם עוד צער). Greek: 'I put upon you no other burden' (οὐ βάλλω ἐφ' ὑμᾶς ἄλλο βάρος). Hebrew uses 'distress' (tsa'ar); Greek uses 'burden' (baros).
Greek adds 'as they speak' (ὡς λέγουσιν) — qualifying that 'depths of Satan' is THEIR terminology. Absent from Hebrew.
translation_notes: 'Teaching of the Adversary' — a curriculum of evil, not mysterious depths. The Hebrew presents a concrete pedagogical danger.

verses.translation: But hold fast{H2388} to what{H2088} you have{H3426} until{H5704} I come{H935}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses תַּחֲזִקוּ (tachaziku — 'hold fast/strengthen', H2388 — root חזק). This is the OT word for courage and tenacity — the verb used when YHWH tells Joshua חֲזַק וֶאֱמָץ ('be strong and courageous', Josh 1:6,7,9). Greek has κρατήσατε ('hold fast/seize'). While these are near-synonyms, the Hebrew חזק carries the Joshua commission resonance — a word of covenant encouragement.
greek_deviations: Close correspondence between Hebrew and Greek here. Greek adds ὃ ἔχετε ('what you have') which matches Hebrew שיש לכם.
textual_notes: Joshua 1:9 — 'Be strong and courageous (חזק ואמץ). Do not be afraid or dismayed, for YHWH your God is with you wherever you go.' The command to 'hold fast' echoes the conquest commission.

verses.translation: And whoever{H4310} overcomes{H5329} — I will give{H5414} nations{H1471} as his inheritance{H5159}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses נַחֲלָה (nachalah — 'inheritance', H5159) — THE Hebrew word for the tribal land allotment in the Promised Land (Josh 13-19, Num 26:53-56, 34:2). Greek has ἐξουσίαν ('authority/power'). A back-translator from Greek would use שִׁלְטוֹן (shilton — 'authority/dominion'), not the land-inheritance nachalah. The Hebrew envisions INHERITING the nations — possessing them as a patrimony; the Greek envisions RULING them — exercising authority. This directly echoes Psalm 2:8 — שְׁאַל מִמֶּנִּי וְאֶתְּנָה גוֹיִם נַחֲלָתֶךָ ('Ask of me and I will give nations as your inheritance'). The Hebrew Revelation QUOTES Psalm 2:8 nearly verbatim (אתנה גוים נחלתו); the Greek paraphrases.

The Hebrew omits entirely 'and keeps my works to the end' (ὁ τηρῶν ἄχρι τέλους τὰ ἔργα μου) which is present in Greek. The Hebrew overcomer simply overcomes; the Greek overcomer must also keep works to the end.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'nations as his inheritance' (nachalah — land patrimony). Greek: 'authority over the nations' (ἐξουσίαν ἐπὶ τῶν ἐθνῶν — governmental power). Different relationship to the nations.
Hebrew omits the condition 'keeps my works to the end' present in Greek.
translation_notes: 'Inheritance' for nachalah — the Promised-Land inheritance concept. The overcomer receives the nations as Abraham's seed received Canaan.
textual_notes: Psalm 2:8 — 'Ask of me and I will give nations as your inheritance (נחלתך), and the ends of the earth as your possession.' The Hebrew Revelation quotes this psalm directly. The next verse (v26) continues the Psalm 2 quotation.

verses.translation: And he shall lead{H5090} them with a rod{H7626} of iron{H1270}, and like a potter's{H3335} vessel{H3627} you shall shatter{H5310} them.

one_way_hebrew: PSALM 2 QUOTATION: The second half — וְכִכְלִי יוֹצֵר תְּנַפְּצֵם ('and like a potter's vessel you shall shatter them') — is nearly VERBATIM from Psalm 2:9b (כִּכְלִי יוֹצֵר תְּנַפְּצֵם). The Hebrew Revelation preserves the Psalm's exact words.

The first half uses יְנַהֵג (yenaheg — 'shall lead/drive', H5090) where Psalm 2:9a has תְּרֹעֵם (tero'em — 'you shall break them', from root רעע H7489). The Hebrew Revelation CHANGES the Psalm: instead of 'break them' (destruction), it says 'lead them' (shepherding). This is a deliberate theological reinterpretation — the rod of iron becomes an instrument of governance, not annihilation. Significantly, the Greek ποιμανεῖ ('shall shepherd') aligns with the Hebrew Revelation's 'lead' rather than with the Psalm's 'break' — suggesting the Greek follows the Hebrew Revelation's reading, not the MT of Psalm 2.

Uses שֵׁבֶט (shevet — 'rod/scepter/tribe', H7626) — a word with triple meaning in Hebrew: (1) a rod/staff, (2) a royal scepter, (3) a tribe of Israel. This triple meaning is uniquely Hebrew and untranslatable. Greek ῥάβδῳ ('rod') captures only one meaning.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'lead them' (ינהג — govern/shepherd). Greek: 'shepherd them' (ποιμανεῖ). Close — both deviate from Psalm 2's 'break them.'
Hebrew: 'you shall shatter them' (תנפצם — 2nd person). Greek: 'they shall be broken' (συντριβήσεται — passive). Different voice.
translation_notes: 'Lead' for yenaheg — not 'break.' The Hebrew Revelation reinterprets Psalm 2's destruction as governance.
'Rod' for shevet carries the triple Hebrew meaning of staff, scepter, and tribe.
textual_notes: Psalm 2:9 (MT) — תְּרֹעֵם בְּשֵׁבֶט בַּרְזֶל כִּכְלִי יוֹצֵר תְּנַפְּצֵם. The LXX of Psalm 2:9 reads ποιμανεῖς ('you will shepherd') instead of 'break,' reading תרעם as from רעה (shepherd) not רעע (break). The Hebrew Revelation's ינהג (lead) represents yet a third reading — neither breaking nor shepherding but leading/driving.

verses.translation: And just as I received{H6901} from my Father{H1}, so I will give{H5414} him the dawn{H7837}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses הַשַּׁחַר (ha-shachar — 'the dawn/daybreak', H7837) where Greek has τὸν ἀστέρα τὸν πρωϊνόν ('the morning star'). The Hebrew gives the DAWN ITSELF — the breaking of light over darkness — not a single star. A back-translator from Greek would write כּוֹכַב הַבֹּקֶר ('star of the morning'), not shachar. The Hebrew is grander: the overcomer receives not a star but dawn — the end of all darkness. Isaiah 14:12 uses the related phrase הֵילֵל בֶּן שָׁחַר ('Helel, son of the Dawn') — the fallen aspirant who sought to climb above God. The true dawn belongs to the overcomer.
Uses אָבִי (avi — 'my Father', H1) — the intimate possessive form expressing filial relationship. The speaker claims sonship to the one from whom authority was received.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'the dawn' (השחר — the breaking of daylight). Greek: 'the morning star' (τὸν ἀστέρα τὸν πρωϊνόν — a specific celestial object). Different gift: all-encompassing dawn vs. a single star.
Hebrew has 'so I will give him the dawn' as a direct continuation. Greek has 'And I will give him the morning star' as a separate sentence/verse.
translation_notes: 'Dawn' for shachar — not 'morning star.' The Hebrew envisions the gift as the breaking of cosmic light, not a single point of light.

Note: The source text has [28] marking a verse division within this text. The content before [28] ('as I received from my Father') and after ('so I will give him the dawn') correspond to standard verses 27b-28.
textual_notes: Isaiah 14:12 — 'How you are fallen from heaven, Helel son of the Dawn (בן שחר)!' The dawn (shachar) that the fallen one lost is now given to the overcomer. Malachi 3:20 (Hebrew; 4:2 English) — 'The sun of righteousness shall rise (וזרחה) with healing in its wings' — uses a related sunrise/dawn image for eschatological vindication.

verses.translation: Whoever{H4310} has{H3426} ears{H241} hears{H8085} what the Spirit{H7307} says{H559} to the assembly{H5712}.

one_way_hebrew: The recurring formula uses singular עֵדָה (edah — 'assembly') throughout the chapter, never the plural. Greek alternates between singular ἐκκλησία (in individual letters) and plural ἐκκλησίαις (in the ears formula of some manuscripts). The Hebrew's consistent singular edah presents each assembly as a singular covenantal community.

As noted in v6: the Hebrew uses dual אָזְנַיִם (oznayim — 'ears') and the present participle שׁוֹמֵעַ (shome'a — 'hears' as a fact), while Greek uses singular οὖς ('ear') and the imperative ἀκουσάτω ('let him hear' as a command). The Hebrew structure declares: having ears entails hearing. The Greek structure commands: having an ear, choose to hear.

chapter_notes.summary: Revelation 2 in Hebrew addresses four assemblies (Ephesus, Zmirinin/Smyrna, Pergamos, Thyatira) using consistent Torah-prophetic vocabulary throughout. The chapter contains at least 20 clear one-way translation markers — cases where the Hebrew could not plausibly derive from the Greek text. The most striking are: (1) גן עדן (Garden of Eden) vs. 'Paradise of God' (v6), (2) עדות טובה (good testimony — an Ark-of-the-Covenant item) vs. 'white stone' (v16), combined with the hidden manna to give the overcomer TWO of the three Ark items, (3) בן יהוה (Son of YHWH) vs. 'Son of God' (v17), (4) נחלה (inheritance — Promised Land concept) vs. 'authority' (v25), (5) שחר (dawn) vs. 'morning star' (v27), and (6) 'remember WHO YOU ARE' vs. 'remember FROM WHERE YOU FELL' (v5). Key recurring Hebrew patterns include: עדה (edah — Mosaic assembly) for 'church' throughout, כה אמר (koh amar — prophetic formula) for each letter, תשובה (teshuvah — return) for 'repentance,' תקוה (tiqvah — hope) where Greek has 'endurance,' and מנורות (menorot — Temple lampstands) for 'lampstands.' The chapter also shows major structural deviations from the Greek: the Nicolaitan commendation is absent from Ephesus and relocated to Pergamos with opposite evaluation (praise in Hebrew, criticism in Greek), false 'prophets' replace false 'apostles' (v2), and 'children of the Adversary' replaces 'synagogue of Satan' (v8). The Hebrew text is consistently more concise than the Greek, omitting several Greek expansions (poverty/riches paradox, eating idol-sacrifices, 'she repented not'). Direct OT quotations include Psalm 2:8-9 (vv25-26), Psalm 149:6 (v11), and Jeremiah 17:10 (v22).
